angle: 14 years of study before the money, versus the author who spent first and died penniless
caption:
In the novel, Edmond Dantès loses 14 years to a lie, and the man who teaches him everything is a fellow prisoner. The author, Alexandre Dumas, built a château named after the book and died penniless. What would you do with 14 years of forced patience?

Sources: Wikipedia, LitCharts, SparkNotes, France Today

slides.heading: Betrayed at 19. Buried for 14 years.
slides.body:
In the novel, Edmond Dantès loses everything to a lie. What he does with those 14 years is the whole story.

And the man who wrote it died penniless.
slides.source: LitCharts summary (age 19, fourteen years); France Today (Dumas died penniless in 1870)

slides.heading: It took one anonymous letter.
slides.body: Danglars wrote it, angry about Dantès' promotion. Fernand sent it, jealous of his fiancée. Caderousse watched and said nothing. Villefort, the prosecutor, burned the proof to protect his own career. Sentence: life in the Château d'If.
slides.source: Wikipedia (EPFL mirror) and LitCharts plot summaries

slides.heading: He nearly starved himself to death.
slides.body:
Years into the sentence, Dantès nearly starved himself to death in the Château d'If.

What stopped it was meeting another prisoner through the wall: Abbé Faria.

The turning point of the whole story was a person, not a plan.
slides.source: LitCharts summary; Wikipedia (EPFL mirror). Last line is commentary.

slides.heading: Prison became his university.
slides.body:
Faria, an Italian priest and scholar, taught him languages, history, economics, philosophy, mathematics, chemistry and the manners of polite society.

He walked in a sailor. He was building into something else.
slides.source: Wikipedia (EPFL mirror) character section. Last two lines are commentary.

slides.heading: Their first escape plan failed.
slides.body:
The wardens fortified the exact weak point they were digging toward.

The escape that worked came after Faria died. Dantès sewed himself into the dead man's sheet, was thrown into the sea, cut himself free and swam to safety.

slides.heading: Faria left him a location, not cash.
slides.body:
Before dying, Faria described a fortune buried on Monte Cristo by Italian nobles in the sixteenth century. Dantès memorized the instructions and found it.

Then he wore three identities, gathered information on each enemy, and ruined them one by one.
slides.source: LitCharts summary (treasure, identities: Count of Monte Cristo, Abbé Busoni, Lord Wilmore)

slides.heading: Then the author built a château named after it.
slides.body:
Alexandre Dumas built the Château de Monte-Cristo in 1846, near Paris. The 1847 housewarming drew an estimated 600 people.

His architect said it would cost several hundred thousand francs. Dumas replied: "I certainly hope so!"
slides.source: France Today; Snippets of Paris (600 guests, July 1847)

slides.heading: Dumas died penniless in 1870.
slides.body:
He was described as poor with money, often living on credit. After the 1848 revolution his finances collapsed, and in 1851, facing bankruptcy, he went into exile in Brussels.

The man who wrote the greatest wealth story could not hold his own.
slides.source: France Today (died penniless 1870); Snippets of Paris (1848, 1851, living on credit). Last line is commentary; SINGLE-SOURCE: 1848/1851 details

slides.heading: The ending rejects revenge.
slides.body:
One reading: the Count gave up playing God and decided that only God can act as Providence.

His last advice to his friends: until the day God reveals the future, all human wisdom is in two words. Wait and hope.
slides.source: SparkNotes (reading of the ending, Ch. 117); LitCharts (farewell). Novel is 1844, public domain.

slides.heading: Dantès had the plan. Dumas had the party.
slides.body:
In the book, 14 years of study came before the money.

In Dumas's life, the spending came first.

Which one are you building toward?
